_comment: Printers are grouped by CLASS, not by model. This is deliberate. The advice that actually changes between machines depends on four things — motion system, extruder type, whether there is an enclosure, and maximum hotend temperature — not on the badge. Grouping this way also keeps us from generating a page per printer model, which would be scaled content abuse and would get the site deindexed. Add a machine by putting it in the examples list of the class it belongs to.

bedslinger-bowden.name: Open bed-slinger, Bowden
quirks: Long Bowden tube means retraction needs to be far longer than a direct-drive machine — typically 4–7 mm against 0.5–2 mm
The moving bed limits useful print speed; tall thin parts wobble at speed and produce ringing
Stock hotends are usually PTFE-lined, which degrades above about 240 °C and releases fumes — this caps the materials you can safely run
Flexible filament is difficult to impossible without an extruder upgrade

bedslinger-direct.name: Open bed-slinger, direct drive
quirks: Short filament path means retraction should be small — starting above about 2 mm usually causes more problems than it solves
Handles flexible filament well, which is the main reason to choose this over Bowden
Still a moving bed, so tall parts remain speed-limited regardless of what the hotend can do
No enclosure means ABS, ASA, PC and nylon will warp or split; PLA and PETG are the comfortable range

i3-direct.name: i3-style, direct drive, open
quirks: Well-tuned stock profiles mean a failure is more likely to be filament or hardware than slicer settings — check moisture and the nozzle first
Input shaping on MK4-class machines allows real speed; older MK3S-class machines do not and will ring if pushed
Add-on enclosures make ABS and ASA workable but watch that the electronics stay cool

corexy-open.name: Open CoreXY
quirks: The bed moves only in Z, so tall parts are far less speed-limited than on a bed-slinger
High achievable acceleration exposes extrusion problems that slower machines hide — under-extrusion often appears only at speed
Usually self-built, so a defect is as likely to be mechanical (belt tension, gantry rack) as it is to be a setting

corexy-enclosed.name: Enclosed CoreXY
quirks: The enclosure that makes ABS and ASA possible actively harms PLA — chamber heat softens parts before they finish cooling. Open the door for PLA
High speed and acceleration mean moisture problems show up as surface defects that look like settings problems
Auto-calibration hides small mechanical faults until they become large ones

delta.name: Delta
quirks: Bed levelling errors show as a dished or domed first layer across the whole plate rather than a tilt — delta calibration is its own skill
Usually Bowden, so retraction behaves like a Bowden bed-slinger
Very fast in X and Y with a fixed bed, which suits tall cylindrical parts
